name: Conversion audit and redesign (homepage, collection, product, cart, checkout or the whole site)
asked_as: why is my conversion rate so low
do a CRO audit of my store
people add to cart but don't buy
my ads get clicks but no sales
make my landing page convert better
outcome: The owner sees the whole path from ad or search to repeat order, with the drop at each step from their own numbers, knows which leak costs the most gross profit and why, and gets either a ranked fix list or a rebuilt page in their brand, each change with its evidence and how it will be measured.
first_principles: Conversion rate belongs to the traffic, not the page. A sitewide rate moves when the mix of cold social, search, returning and mobile visitors moves, so never judge a page until it is cut by source, device and new versus returning. The unit that matters is gross profit per session, set against what that session cost to buy.

The leak is the step that drops most against the store's own best cell (its best source, device or landing page), not against an industry average. Benchmarks only say where to look. Then put the best page next to the worst page on like-for-like traffic and ask what one has that the other lacks: a promise, a first screen, proof, a delivery date, a price point, stock.

Many 'page problems' live upstream or downstream of the page. An ad that promises one thing and lands on another, the wrong products in the first rows, sold-out sizes, a slow first load, surprise shipping cost, failed payments or COD friction. Fix the cause where it lives; a prettier page does not fix a broken promise.

Testing spends traffic. Below about 1,000 weekly visitors to a page, or about 300 orders a month, a split test cannot read the 1 to 5% lifts that mature pages really get. Ship evidence-backed changes, read them before and after against a control, and save tests for big swings the traffic can read. Repairs never wait for a test.

Fix when the page is close to the store's best cell and the leaks are local. Rebuild when the page has the wrong job for its traffic (cold buyers on a product page that needs explaining, a homepage that is just a catalogue), when three or more leaks share one root cause, or when the theme blocks the fixes. A rebuild keeps everything the best page has already proved.

Every recommendation carries two pieces of evidence (a number plus behaviour or the buyer's own words), its gross profit a month at stake, its chance of working and its build cost. Rank on that, never on how many best practices a page fails, and never on case-study lifts.

questions.ask: Should I map the whole path from ad to repeat order, one page type, or one page?
questions.why: The page an owner suspects is often not where the money leaks; scope sets how much data to pull and whether a rebuild is on the table.

options.label: The whole path
options.pro: finds the real leak, which is often upstream or at checkout
options.con: more data to pull before the first fix

options.label: One page type (all product pages, say)
options.pro: fixes one template across many pages
options.con: can miss a leak on another step

options.label: One page
options.pro: fastest, good for a key landing page
options.con: a fix there may move little if traffic or checkout is the problem

questions.default: The whole path, then depth on the step that loses the most gross profit
skip_if: brief names one page and the funnel confirms it is the biggest leak
the owner only wants a page rebuilt from a reference
questions.settle_with_data: Build the funnel by device first. If one step's drop is far worse than the store's own best cell and costs the most gross profit, say so and go deep there, whatever the brief named.

questions.ask: What should this win: more orders from the same traffic, bigger orders, or profit on paid traffic?
questions.why: Conversion work, order value work (bundles, thresholds) and paid landing work are different jobs with different pages.

options.label: More orders
options.pro: the usual lever
options.con: can lower order value if it leans on discounts

options.label: Bigger orders
options.pro: lifts profit without more traffic
options.con: needs real bundle and threshold logic, not a bar

options.label: Profit on paid traffic
options.pro: decides whether ad spend can grow
options.con: narrower: the pages ads land on

questions.default: Gross profit per session, which covers all three
questions.settle_with_data: If paid traffic is most sessions and gross profit per session (conversion rate x gross profit per order) is below its cost per click, profit on paid traffic is the goal. If the order-value spread shows a clear peak just under the free-shipping line, bigger orders is in play.

questions.ask: Can you give me read access to GA4 and your store analytics, or send exports?
questions.why: Landing page, device and source cuts need analytics; without them the audit rests on ad counts, a phone walk-through and reviews, and says so.

options.label: Read access
options.pro: every cut I need, fastest
options.con: a few minutes to add a viewer

options.label: Exports
options.pro: no access shared
options.con: I send a list of reports; slower to go deeper

options.label: Neither
options.pro: start today
options.con: conclusions marked directional until numbers arrive

questions.default: Exports: I send the exact list, and start the phone walk-through and review reading meanwhile
skip_if: a connector to GA4 or the store already works

questions.ask: Who will build the changes: you in the theme editor, a developer, or should I hand over ready-made sections?
questions.why: It decides how big the fixes can be and whether a rebuild is realistic.

options.label: Me, in the theme editor
options.pro: no cost
options.con: limits fixes to what the theme allows

options.label: A developer
options.pro: any fix, including a rebuild
options.con: costs hours; I size each fix in build time

options.label: Ready-made sections from you
options.pro: drop-in, built on a theme copy
options.con: needs draft access to an unpublished theme

questions.default: Theme-editor fixes first, plus ready-made sections for anything bigger
questions.settle_with_data: Read the theme and installed apps: if the theme has the sections a fix needs, the editor is enough.

data_map.question: Where does the path from landing to purchase drop most, and on which device?
data_map.data: Sessions, product view, add to cart, begin checkout, purchase by device and by new versus returning, 90 days and the same window a year ago
data_map.where: GA4 purchase journey or funnel exploration; Shopify conversion breakdown
data_map.if_missing: Meta landing page view, add to cart, checkout and purchase counts for ad traffic, plus store carts, checkouts and orders

data_map.question: Which landing pages hold visitors best and worst on like-for-like traffic?
data_map.data: Sessions, engagement rate (bounce is its inverse), add to cart rate, purchase rate and revenue per session by landing page, within one source and device, only pages with about 300+ sessions
data_map.where: GA4 Landing page report with session source and device; Shopify sessions and conversion by landing page
data_map.if_missing: Meta landing page view to purchase per landing URL

data_map.question: Does the page keep the ad's promise, and does it load?
data_map.data: Per ad: link clicks, landing page views, add to carts, purchases, landing URL; the ad's copy and visual
data_map.where: Meta connector or Ads Manager export
data_map.if_missing: the store's live ads in the Ad Library, opened next to their landing pages on a phone

data_map.question: Which products get looked at but not added to cart?
data_map.data: Item views, add to carts and purchases by product and device; price, stock by variant, review count
data_map.where: GA4 item reports; Shopify product analytics
data_map.if_missing: product page walk-through for the top sellers and top-traffic products

data_map.question: Where inside cart and checkout do buyers leave?
data_map.data: begin_checkout, add_shipping_info, add_payment_info, purchase; abandoned checkouts by step and pincode or region; payment success by method
data_map.where: GA4 funnel exploration; Shopify abandoned checkouts; payment gateway report
data_map.if_missing: a test-mode checkout run on a phone and the abandoned checkout list

data_map.question: What does an order earn, and does the first order lead to a second?
data_map.data: Gross profit per order, the order-value spread and its peaks, discount share, repeat rate and time to second order by first product and first landing page
data_map.where: Shopify order export plus SKU costs
data_map.if_missing: average order value and the owner's margin, marked rough

data_map.question: What do buyers actually do on the leaking page?
data_map.data: Scroll reach at 25, 50 and 75%; click share per element; dead and rage clicks; quick backs; recordings of lost buyers versus buyers
data_map.if_missing: timed phone walk-through of five buyer paths

data_map.question: What doubt stops them, in their words?
data_map.data: Top pre-sale questions, 1 to 3 star review themes, return reasons, 'what almost stopped you' answers
data_map.where: helpdesk, chats, review app, returns app, survey
data_map.if_missing: public reviews of the store and its two closest rivals

data_map.question: Is speed costing sales on phones?
data_map.data: Field LCP, INP and CLS at the 75th percentile per template on mobile; app and script count
data_map.where: PageSpeed Insights field data; theme and app list
data_map.if_missing: three repeated lab runs per template, labelled lab

data_map.question: Is the traffic real?
data_map.data: Store sessions against GA4 sessions; sessions with no interaction by source and country
data_map.if_missing: judge on GA4 or on orders only

tools: node tools/ask-knowledge.mjs "<the leaking step> on <device>" --module CRO,LPG,SPD,CXP
look_for: Split the change first: revenue = sessions x conversion x order value; a small fall in two parts compounds and is often noise, so chase only what moved beyond its usual swing.
Mix before page: if the sitewide rate fell but each source-and-device rate held, the traffic changed (more cold social, more mobile, a new country), not the page.

Claims match across ads, product pages and policy pages: material words (natural, lab-grown, hallmarked, certified), offers (EMI or pay in parts versus layaway or pay-first plans, free shipping, gift packing), return and exchange terms, prices and delivery dates. Read the live ads (Ad Library or the connector), the product pages and the policy pages side by side. A mismatch (a lab-grown piece badged 'natural', 'EMI' in the ad but a pay-first plan on the site) is a trust leak and a legal risk: fix it before any test.

Payment terms, exactly: for each term in the ads or on the site (EMI, no-cost EMI, pay later, instalments, gold savings or layaway plans), write who pays how much, when, and when the piece ships. EMI means the buyer gets the piece now and pays a lender over months; a plan where the buyer pays first and gets the piece later is a savings or layaway plan, never EMI. An ad that says EMI for a pay-first plan is a mismatch at the moment of buying: it goes at the top of the fixes.

The path from an ad inside the Instagram and Facebook apps: most paid social clicks open in their in-app browser, where Google sign-in is blocked, saved cards and autofill are missing, and some payment apps fail to hand back. Walk it on a phone from a real ad to the order page: forced sign-in, a social login that fails, a payment that does not return.

Best versus worst landing page within the same source and device: list what the best one's first screen has that the worst lacks (the promise, price, proof type, delivery date, offer, product in view). That difference is hypothesis one.

The step with the biggest drop against the store's own best cell; benchmarks only flag where to look (view product 50 to 70%, view to cart 12 to 20%, cart to checkout 40 to 60%, checkout to purchase 45 to 60%).
Clicks that never become landing page views, well below the account's own rate for some ads: the page is slow or breaks before it loads. That is a speed fix, not a copy fix.
High click-through ads with low landing-page-view-to-cart on the same URL: the page does not continue the ad's angle or persona; each angle needs a first screen that leads with that one benefit.
A weak product view rate with a healthy view-to-cart rate: the leak is the menu, the first rows of collections or search, not the product page.
Low view-to-cart on a few products only: price against rivals, sold-out key sizes, photos, under about 80 reviews, or a missing delivery date for those items, not the template.

Cart to checkout weak: surprise costs (fees above about 10% of order value), a discount box that sends buyers hunting for codes, a free-shipping line set from the mean order value instead of the peaks of the order spread.
Checkout to purchase weak: payment failures by method, OTP or COD friction, pincode and delivery checks, forced accounts; read the gateway's success rates before touching copy.

Scroll map: where half the visitors are gone, and whether price, proof and risk reducers sit above that line; elements under about 1% of clicks are clutter; elements with many clicks but few visitors reaching them should move up.
Recordings: dead clicks on images, price or size, back and forth between size chart and variants, quick backs from product to collection mean missing information, not missing persuasion.
The top pre-sale questions and top return reasons are missing page content; 1 to 3 star reviews name the promise the page made and the product didn't keep.
Repeat side: which first product and first landing page produce second orders; a page that converts on a deep discount and brings no repeat buyers is buying one-time customers.
Gross profit per session against cost per click by source: if paid traffic earns less per session than it costs, no ad tweak helps until the page or the offer lifts.
Data traps before any claim: bot sessions in store counts, GA4 key events that are not purchases, sale days in the window, COD orders that never deliver.

hypothesis_patterns.pattern: A traffic-mix shift, not a page problem
hypothesis_patterns.evidence: per-source and per-device rates flat while the share of cold social or mobile sessions rose
hypothesis_patterns.bet: judge pages per segment; move the work to message match or the offer for the new traffic

hypothesis_patterns.pattern: The best page has what the worst lacks
hypothesis_patterns.evidence: two landing pages with comparable source and device traffic far apart on engagement and add to cart; the best shows an element the worst does not (delivery date, review count by the title, the ad's promise as the headline)
hypothesis_patterns.bet: carry the element across; read before and after against the untouched pages

hypothesis_patterns.pattern: The ad's promise breaks on landing
hypothesis_patterns.evidence: ads with strong click-through and weak landing-page-view-to-cart on the same URL; the ad's angle is not in the first screen
hypothesis_patterns.bet: a first screen per angle, or a page built for that traffic

hypothesis_patterns.evidence: low product view rate, exits from home and collections, dead clicks on the menu, failed site searches
hypothesis_patterns.bet: menu, first rows and search fixed before any product page work

hypothesis_patterns.evidence: cart to checkout or checkout to purchase far below the store's best cell; abandoned checkouts bunch at shipping or payment; one payment method fails often
hypothesis_patterns.bet: show full cost and a padded delivery date early; fix the failing method; repairs ship now

hypothesis_patterns.pattern: The page leaves the main doubt unanswered
hypothesis_patterns.evidence: the top pre-sale question or return reason is not answered on the page, or only below where most visitors stop scrolling
hypothesis_patterns.bet: answer it where the doubt arises: by the size picker, under the button

hypothesis_patterns.evidence: click-to-landing-page-view loss; mobile LCP above 2.5 seconds at the 75th percentile; many app scripts
hypothesis_patterns.bet: speed fixes first: hero image, then third-party scripts

hypothesis_patterns.pattern: The wrong page for the traffic (revamp)
hypothesis_patterns.evidence: cold traffic on a product page that needs explaining, with high bounce and long scroll but few carts; three or more leaks with one root cause
hypothesis_patterns.bet: rebuild the page, or build a listicle, story or angle page for that traffic, and keep the current page for warm visitors

decisions.ask: Fix the current page, rebuild it, or add a new page for one kind of traffic?

options.label: Targeted fixes
options.pro: fast, low risk, each change readable on its own
options.con: caps the gain when the structure is the problem
options.when: the page sits close to the store's best cell and the leaks are local

options.label: Rebuild around the main doubt
options.pro: the biggest possible lift; fixes a shared root cause in one go
options.con: more build time, harder to say which part worked, can dip before it rises
options.when: a big gap to the best cell, three or more leaks with one cause, or a theme that blocks the fixes

options.label: Keep it, add a page for one source
options.pro: protects what works for warm visitors, matches cold traffic
options.con: one more page to keep up to date
options.when: one source (often cold social) converts far below the others on the same page

decisions.recommend: Pick from the gap: fixes when the page is within reach of the store's best cell; a rebuild when the gap is large and the causes share a root; a new page when one source is the outlier. Name the two numbers that decided it.

decisions.ask: How do we prove each change worked?

options.label: Ship and read before and after
options.pro: no waiting for traffic
options.con: weaker proof; season and ad changes can muddy it
options.when: under about 1,000 weekly visitors to the page or about 300 orders a month; read against a control (another device, untouched pages, the same weeks last year)

options.label: Split test the big change
options.pro: real proof of the lift
options.con: weeks of traffic, one test at a time, no checkout tests on standard Shopify, no price splits on one product
options.when: the page's own traffic reaches the sample for the expected lift within about four weeks

options.label: Ship repairs now, test the one bold bet
options.pro: speed where it is safe, proof where it counts
options.con: only one idea gets real proof
options.when: middle traffic, or a mix of broken things and one big idea

decisions.recommend: Set by the store's monthly orders and the page's own traffic: under about 30 orders a month, research and ship; 30 to 300, one bold test sized for a 20%+ lift; 300 to 3,000, regular tests; repairs always ship. Show the sample sum.

rules: Every before image is a real, unclipped screenshot of today's page on a phone; every after image is labelled a mockup until it is live.
Every fix names its hypothesis, two pieces of evidence, its gross profit a month, its chance of working, its build hours, and how it will be read.
A page with no leak is marked fine; there is no quota of findings or tests per page.
Plan on 1 to 5% lifts unless the store's own tests show more; case-study lifts are the top of a range, never the plan.
Repairs ship without a test. No split tests on standard Shopify checkout, and never two prices for one product.

Proof on any page must be true: real reviews with names and sources, real deadlines and stock; no invented counters, badges or timers, and no hidden costs (Indian dark-pattern rules and US claim rules apply).
A rebuild keeps what the store's best page has proved and borrows only structure from other brands, never their words, images, icons or fonts.
New words on the page come from the org context and the buyers' own words, in the brand's language and register.
Mockups are built from HTML with the brand's real words; run copy-check and the consistency check on the mockup source folder before rendering, so a banned word ('sale') never reaches an image.

checks: Sessions x conversion x order value multiplies back to the revenue change in the summary.
Every rate in a finding names its source, period, device and traffic segment.
Rebuilt pages pass a phone check at 390 px: price, button and risk reducer in the first screen, no layout shift from apps, hero image not lazy-loaded.
Claim table filled: every material, offer, return and price claim checked across the live ads, the product pages and the policy pages.
The in-app browser path from a real ad was walked on a phone, and sign-in and payment were tried there.
Payment terms table: each term, the exact mechanism (who pays, when, when it ships) from the site's own page, and every ad or page that names it.
senior_review: Could a change in traffic mix explain this finding instead of the page?
Did I compare the best and worst pages on like-for-like traffic, and name what one has that the other lacks?
Is the top fix where the most gross profit sits, or only the most visible flaw?
Did the evidence call for a rebuild, and did I say plainly why or why not?
Is test versus ship matched to this store's traffic, with the sample sum shown?
Can the owner build this in the hours they have?
Does every new line sound like the brand and rest on a true fact?
What did I assume that the data contradicts?
Does anything we say in ads, on the page or in a policy contradict another, and would a buyer feel misled?
Does every payment word (EMI, pay later, instalments) mean the same thing in the ad, on the product page and at checkout?
Does any cut or fix rest on a short window that the 90-day numbers contradict?

files: A one-screen summary as one branded HTML page: the leakiest step and device, the top three fixes with gross profit a month, any claim that does not match across ads, site and policy, and the one thing to do this week.
The funnel map as a sheet and CSV: source to landing page to product to cart to checkout to purchase to repeat, by device and source, with the drop and gross profit at each step.
A best-versus-worst page table: the pages, their traffic, their rates, and the elements one has that the other lacks.
A claim table: claim, where it appears, match or mismatch, the fix and the risk.
A ranked findings CSV: finding, evidence (two), fix, gross profit a month, chance, build hours, ship or test, owner, how it is read.
Real before screenshots and labelled after mockups (PNG), or the rebuilt page as HTML plus Shopify section files on an unpublished theme.
A test plan per test, or a before-and-after reading plan with its control and read date.
A short deck in the brand's colours for the owner or their team.
